web_title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Multiples, Reverse DCF and Peers
book_title: Why the Price Is What It Is
question: What is the market already paying for at ₹187, and does that price leave room for what the business has actually shown?

epigraph.quote: It would change a little bit.
epigraph.author: Stallion management, answering whether the FY27 contribution of about ₹250 crore from the new plant still held, Q1 FY27 earnings call, 17 August 2026 [9]

web_blocks.html: Start with the price, because everything else in this chapter has to explain it. At ₹187.12 on 13 November 2026 the market values Stallion at about ₹2,172 crore, using the share count implied by the company’s own market value and price [14]. Take out the net cash and the operating business is priced at about ₹1,773 crore. We build the multiples below from the audited statements and the Screener series, and we say plainly where the vendor snapshot disagrees.

web_blocks.takeaway: The vendor P/E figures run from 35x to 50x because they use different earnings bases. We use the reported-EPS figure, 47.5x, and show the spread so you can see how much the answer depends on the method.

web_blocks.html: The trailing P/E is the figure most readers see first. On reported EPS of ₹3.94 for the last four quarters, the stock trades at 47.5 times earnings. That number is pushed around by two quarters. The June 2026 quarter earned ₹18.6 crore at an operating margin of 18.2 percent. The September 2026 quarter earned ₹2.5 crore at an operating margin of 2.2 percent, with a tax charge of 57 percent [14]. Neither quarter is a trend. The sensible base is the year: about ₹43 to ₹44 crore of profit, and a price of roughly 40 to 50 times that depending on the cash treatment and the share count.

Cash is a fair part of the story, and it is worth separating. Net cash is about ₹400 crore, or ₹34.43 a share, based on the March 2026 audited balance sheet [1]. An investor paying ₹187.12 is therefore paying about ₹34 for cash and about ₹153 for the operating business. The cash is real. The question is what the operating business earns on the ₹153, and that depends on the plants in chapter 5.

web_blocks.title: Reverse DCF: what the price already assumes

web_blocks.html: A reverse DCF asks what growth today’s price needs. We set a 12.5 percent cost of equity, 5 percent growth after ten years, and ask what ten-year profit growth makes the discounted value equal the operating value of ₹1,773 crore. The base is FY26 net profit of ₹43.8 crore. We use profit rather than free cash flow because FY26 free cash flow was negative: operating cash flow of ₹39.4 crore less ₹49.3 crore of plant, equipment and work-in-progress spending [1][23]. Profit is an imperfect base for a company still building capacity, and that is a limit of this method, not a detail to skip.

web_blocks.caption: Reverse DCF for Stallion at ₹187.12: cost of equity 12.5%, terminal growth 5%, ten-year horizon [1][14][23]

web_blocks.takeaway: At ₹187 the market is paying for profit to compound at about 20 percent a year for a decade, and for sales to reach about five times the FY26 level at a normal margin.

web_blocks.html: That is a large ask. Management’s own FY28 target, if met, takes sales above ₹1,100 crore [9]. That would make the business about 2.5 times its FY26 size within two years. The reverse DCF says the price needs the growth to continue for ten years, not stop at a plateau. The plants are the first step on that path, not the whole path, and the price already assumes the first step works.

We value the business on FY28 profit, which is the earliest year in which the current plant plans would show up in the accounts. Each scenario sets a revenue level and a net margin, applies a 30 times multiple to profit, and adds net cash of ₹34.43 a share. The 30 times multiple is generous for a business that earned a 6 percent margin in its bear case, and we test it directly below.

web_blocks.caption: Stallion FY28 scenario values at a 30x multiple plus net cash per share (₹ crore unless stated) [9][23]
rows: ₹700 crore (27% a year, below the 30 to 35% guidance)
web_blocks.takeaway: The base case assumes a 27 percent revenue CAGR, which is below the 30 to 35 percent a year that management has guided [9]. We haircut the guidance in the base case, and we do not treat the bull case as the midpoint.

web_blocks.html: The bear case is the sensitive one. Valued at 15 times earnings instead of 30, its value falls from ₹101 to about ₹68 a share, which is 64 percent below today’s price. We keep 30 times in the table so the three scenarios compare like for like, and we show the 15 times figure here so you can see how much of the bear case depends on the multiple. The probability weighting and the decision are in chapter 9.

The base margin needs a second look. The trailing twelve months show profit of ₹43 crore on sales of ₹472 crore, a net margin of about 9 percent [14], so the 11 percent base assumes the margin rises by about two points. Chapter 2 gives the mechanism: the company's own plant should earn more per kilogram than bought-in product. The sources do not quantify that uplift. At an 8 percent base margin, the base value falls from ₹233 to about ₹179 and the weighted value from ₹226.9 to about ₹202.5. From ₹159.79 that weighted value is about 12.6 percent a year, at the hurdle rather than above it. The base margin is the assumption that most needs testing.

web_blocks.title: Peers: the same industry, three different prices

web_blocks.caption: Stallion against the three listed peers in its prospectus set: snapshot valuation, profitability and Stage 2 status (13 November 2026) [32][33][34][35]
web_blocks.takeaway: The Stallion row uses the vendor snapshot. Its TradingView P/E of 35.0x, operating margin of 14.9% and missing growth and price-to-book fields do not match the Screener basis used in our calculation: 47.5x trailing EPS, an 11.2% trailing operating margin, +4% trailing sales growth and 3.05x book [14][24]. The table is a cross-check, not the valuation.

web_blocks.html: The three peers the prospectus used answer a different question: how the market prices fluorochemical businesses that earn more per rupee of sales. Gujarat Fluorochemicals (FLUOROCHEM) trades at 76 times trailing earnings on an operating margin of 17.4 percent. Navin Fluorine (NAVINFLUOR) trades at 56 times on a 30.3 percent margin and 46 percent revenue growth. SRF trades at 32 times on an 18.8 percent margin [33][34][35]. Each of those multiples is a bet on growth and margin that Stallion has not yet shown.

Stallion sits in the middle on the vendor P/E and above SRF on our reported-EPS basis, while earning lower margins and returns. Its trailing sales growth is 4 percent, against 19.7 percent for SRF [14][33]. Its return on equity is 8.9 percent, against 16.0 percent for SRF [14][33]. The market is not paying for Stallion’s trailing profit. It is paying for plants that are not yet running, and the peer set makes that visible. Any relative case for Stallion has to rest on the plant ramp, not on today’s peer-relative earnings.

There is one caution about history. The snapshot carries no multi-year valuation band for Stallion, so we cannot say whether 47 times is high or low against the company’s own record. We do not invent a band. What we can say is that the ex-cash multiple of 41 times on trailing profit, and about 23 times on our base-case FY28 profit, leaves little room for a plant that starts late.

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR’S REFLECTION
paragraphs: A price is a forecast in disguise. The reverse DCF tells you the forecast you have to believe to justify today’s price. That is useful because the arithmetic is hard to argue with. Here the forecast is about a decade of roughly 20 percent profit growth, and the nearest evidence for it is plants that have not yet started.

That does not make the stock a sell. It makes the timing of the evidence the thing to watch, and it makes the price something we need to test against the cash flows and the chart in the next two chapters.

book_paragraphs: Now the question most readers wait for: is the price reasonable? I will answer it with arithmetic, not with a feeling about the stock. Start with what ₹187 buys. At this price the market values Stallion at about 2,172 crore, using the share count implied by the company’s market value [14]. Of that, about 400 crore is net cash, roughly 34 rupees a share. So the operating business is priced at about 1,773 crore, or about 153 rupees a share.

Keep the cash separate from the business. Most of it came from the rights issue, and it sits in bank deposits and bank balances [1]. A rupee of cash is worth a rupee. A rupee of profit is worth whatever the market will pay for it, and that depends on whether the profit lasts.

The trailing earnings look expensive. On reported earnings of 3.94 rupees a share for the last four quarters, the stock trades at about 47 times. Two quarters explain most of the swing. June 2026 earned about 18.6 crore at an operating margin of 18 percent. September 2026 earned about 2.5 crore at an operating margin of 2 percent, with a tax charge of 57 percent [14]. You should not average those into a verdict. You should ask why September was so weak, and the sources I read did not give a full answer.

A reverse DCF is the tool I use to turn a price into a question. You set a required return, a long-run growth rate and a number of years, and then ask what growth the price needs. I used a 12.5 percent cost of equity, 5 percent growth after ten years, and the FY26 profit of 43.8 crore as the starting point. I did not use free cash flow, because FY26 free cash flow was negative after plant spending [1][23]. That is a weakness of the method, and I want you to see it before you see the answer.

The answer is that the price needs profit to grow at about 20 percent a year for ten years. Ten years of that compounding turns 43.8 crore into about 265 crore. At an 11 percent net margin, that is about 2,400 crore of sales, more than five times FY26. Put that next to management’s own target for FY28, sales above 1,100 crore [9], and you can see the gap. The market is paying for a plant programme to work, and then to keep working.

Now the scenarios. I value the business two years out, on FY28 profit. The bear case has sales flat at 430 crore and a 6 percent net margin. The base case has sales of 700 crore, which is about 27 percent a year growth and sits below the 30 to 35 percent a year that management has guided [9]. It also has an 11 percent margin. The bull case has sales of 1,100 crore and a 14 percent margin, which is management’s own figure. Each case gets a 30 times multiple on profit, plus the net cash per share.

The results are a bear value of about 101 rupees, a base value of about 233 and a bull value of about 432. The bull value is more than twice the price. The bear value is 46 percent below it. Notice that the bear case uses a 30 times multiple, which is generous for a business that earned a 6 percent margin in its weak year. At 15 times, the bear value falls to about 68 rupees, and that is the number I would want you to hold in your head when you hear the word bear.

Then the peers. Gujarat Fluorochemicals trades at about 76 times trailing earnings on a margin of 17 percent. Navin Fluorine trades at about 56 times on a margin of 30 percent and growth of 46 percent. SRF trades at about 32 times on an 18.8 percent margin on the vendor basis [33][34][35]. Stallion is not cheap against SRF. On reported earnings it is priced higher, and it earns lower margins and a lower return on equity. The market is paying for what the plants will do, not for what the company has done.

So the price is not obviously wrong, and it is not obviously cheap either. It assumes a plant ramp, and the next chapter asks what the tape says about whether buyers believe it. Chapter 9 then weighs the two sides against each other and puts a number on the expected return.

Notice how much the answer depends on the method. The vendor sites show price-to-earnings ratios of 35 times, 47 times and 50 times for the same share price, and none of them is wrong on its own terms. One divides the price by reported earnings per share. Another divides market value by profit. A third uses a different earnings base altogether. When the number moves that much with the method, the sensible move is to pick one basis, say what it is, and show the others, which is what this chapter does.

The ex-cash view is the one I trust most for this company, because the cash is large relative to the business. Strip out about 400 crore of net cash and the operating business is priced at about 1,773 crore. On trailing profit that is about 41 times. On the FY28 profit in our base case it is about 23 times. The difference is the bet on the plants. If the plants deliver the base case, today's price looks less stretched in two years. If they do not, the multiple stays high on a profit that has not grown.

A reader might ask why I do not simply compare Stallion with a list of cheap chemical stocks. Cheapness is a statement about the market's expectations, not about the business. The three peers in the prospectus are priced for growth and margins that Stallion has not shown. Matching their multiples would mean paying today for a margin that has not appeared. The useful question is not whether Stallion is cheap against them, but whether its own plants can close the gap, and on what timetable.

Before you move on, write down the number that matters most: the FY28 sales figure the company actually reports, set against 700 crore and 1,100 crore. That single line will tell you more about the price than any multiple in the table.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR’S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Write the FY28 sales target next to today’s price. If the price needs about 2,400 crore of sales at a ten-year growth path, you are not buying what the company earns today. You are buying the next ten years of plants, and you should price that risk on purpose.
